title: An unexpected activist emerged to help block a $5 billion data center in Maryland

sections.title: Conversation 1
sections.scene: A student journalist interviews a community organizer about local resistance to a proposed industrial facility.

script.en: Thanks for meeting me, Mr. Alvarez. I'm writing a piece for the campus paper on how residents here are responding to the proposed logistics hub. Can you walk me through what got you involved?

Sure. About two years ago, I read a notice in the local paper—almost missed it—about a zoning hearing for a massive warehouse complex on the old fairground site. It was going to cover nearly a hundred acres, with round-the-clock truck traffic.
And that was close to where you live?

Less than half a mile. My kids walk to school past that site. So I went to the hearing, mostly to listen, and I was stunned. The developers presented these glossy renderings, but when residents asked about air quality and noise, the answers were vague.

Gradually. First it was just a handful of neighbors meeting in my kitchen. We drafted a petition, went door to door. It took months, but we gathered about three thousand signatures. That got the council's attention.

They imposed a temporary moratorium—six months—while they commissioned an independent impact study. That felt like a real victory. But then the developers came back with a revised proposal, slightly smaller, and some council members started wavering.

Honestly, the study. It found that the site sits on a floodplain and that truck emissions would push particulate levels above federal limits near two elementary schools. Once that was public, the support for the project collapsed.
Not officially. The developer withdrew the application, but they own the land. They could try again. That's why we're pushing for a permanent zoning change. We can't celebrate too early.
What would you say to students who feel these local fights don't matter?
I'd say local decisions shape your daily life more than most national headlines. And you don't need to be a homeowner to have a stake. Renters breathe the same air.

script.en: Across the United States, a quiet but determined form of activism is reshaping local politics: residents are organizing against the rapid expansion of hyperscale data centers. These vast facilities, which power cloud computing and artificial intelligence, consume enormous amounts of electricity and water for cooling, and their growing presence has begun to alarm communities that were once expected to welcome them. While they promise tax revenue and jobs, they also bring noise, diesel emissions from backup generators, and strains on local infrastructure that residents say are rarely disclosed in advance. The response has been swift. According to one estimate, communities have secured roughly five hundred moratoriums on data center construction nationwide, a figure that reflects how quickly ordinary people have learned to navigate zoning boards and municipal hearings. Many of these campaigns are led by ordinary citizens with no prior organizing experience—renters, retirees, and parents concerned about air quality near schools. Their concerns are not merely aesthetic. A single hyperscale campus can demand as much electricity as a small city, and its water consumption can rival that of thousands of households, placing pressure on grids and aquifers already stressed by climate change. Yet the issue is not one-sided. Local governments facing budget shortfalls often view data centers as a reliable source of property tax revenue, and when projects are paused or blocked, some officials warn of cuts to public services. This tension has produced unusual alliances and heated debates at council meetings, where residents and officials clash over how to balance economic need with environmental health. What distinguishes this wave of activism is its demographic breadth. Organizers are increasingly connecting their local fights to broader questions of environmental justice, arguing that low-income and minority communities are disproportionately burdened by industrial development. As one activist put it, the right to clean air and water belongs to everyone. Whether these movements will permanently alter how data centers are sited remains uncertain, but they have already changed the conversation.

sections.title: An Unlikely Activist Takes On a Data Center
sections.passage:
When Taylor Frazier McCollum learned that a $5 billion data center was proposed for the site of a demolished mall less than a mile from her apartment, her reaction was immediate and blunt. The project, if built, would occupy more than 80 acres of vacant land in Prince George's County, Maryland. To her, the prospect of water-polluting, diesel-generating facilities operating beside homes, schools, and playgrounds defied common sense.

Frazier McCollum is not a homeowner. In 2024, she and her young daughter were evicted from their apartment after her wages were cut. That personal upheaval might seem to place her outside the typical profile of a land-use activist, who usually fights to protect a cherished property. Yet it was precisely her precarious circumstances that propelled her into organizing. She launched a petition that ultimately gathered over 25,000 signatures, which in turn led to widely attended protests and multiple local moratoriums on data centers throughout the county. The campaign succeeded in blocking the project, which had been scheduled to break ground between 2026 and 2027.

The struggle thrust Frazier McCollum into the forefront of local politics. She attended county meetings, testified before Maryland legislators, and endorsed political candidates. She found herself in an unlikely coalition of socialists, environmentalists, residents angry about rising electric bills, and neighbors new to organizing. Her message has since traveled beyond Maryland; with grants and support, she has taken her campaign to Black communities fighting data center growth in Atlanta, Memphis, and even Zambia.

Yet the pause on data centers has generated unease in Prince George's County. Some officials worry about declining tax revenue. A local Six Flags theme park closed last year, the NFL's Washington Commanders announced plans to return to neighboring Washington, D.C., and thousands of federal workers have lost their jobs. The county now faces a budget deficit. In September, when Frazier McCollum appeared at a council meeting to advocate for a fund for roof repairs, Council member Wanika Fisher reminded her that the county needs development. Fisher acknowledged that a data center may not be the answer but insisted the hard conversation is worth having.

With the Landover project on hold, Frazier McCollum now seeks a full ban on that and other data center projects. She frames her fight in broader terms: the right to water, clean air, and a place to live. As her grandfather, Lacy McCollum Jr., puts it, people like Taylor jump out front so that those behind them can make progress. Whether her campaign will permanently alter how data centers are sited remains uncertain, but it has already changed the terms of the debate.

It felt like something that wasn't ever going to end." Taylor Frazier McCollum in front of her grandfather's home, where she lived when she heard about the proposed data center site less than a mile away in Landover, Md.

And I'm not saying that a data center is the answer, but I'm saying it's worth the hard discussion." With the Landover project on hold, Frazier McCollum now wants a full ban on that and other data center projects.
